nodes.title: The time series
nodes.content:
Naive: the \textcolor{red}{TIME SERIES} is a sequence of obs taken over time (see fig) \[ y_{1:T} = (y_1, \dots, y_T) \]

Better: a time series is a *Stochastic Process* (Y_t, t $\ge$ 0): a sequence of random vectors (a multidipensional random variable) indexed by t. 

Note:
- To specify the processm you need to write probability law P. 
- Each observed value is a specific realization of the process.

nodes.title: Aims of time series analysis
Time series decomposition
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TIME SERIES DECOMPOSITION}}

View $Y_t$ as composed of: a \textbf{Trend}, a \textbf{Seasonal} comp., a \textbf{cycle}, and an \textbf{Erratic} comp.

\textbf{Additive}:\quad $Y_t = T_t + S_t + C_t + E_t$

\textbf{Multiplicative}:\quad $Y_t = T_t \cdot S_t \cdot C_t \cdot E_t$

note $\log$ transforms a multiplicative decomposition into an additive one

\textbf{Diagnostic:} if the seasonal swing grows with the level of the series, prefer the multiplicative form (or model $\log Y_t$ additively).

nodes.title: Fitting a trend
Detrending
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{DETRENDING}}

Having fitted $\widehat{T}_t$, write
\[ y_t = \widehat{T}_t + E_t, \quad t = 2, \dots, n. \]
Remove the trend to obtain the de-trended series:
\[ y_t^{\text{detrended}} = y_t - \widehat{T}_t. \]

nodes.title: Fitting a seasonal component
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{FITTING A SEASONAL COMPONENT}}

For $Y_t = S_t + E_t$ (purely seasonal, no trend; assume mean zero, $\bar{y}_t = 0$):

\textbf{1. Seasonal factors.} For monthly data introduce $\alpha_{\text{Jan}}, \alpha_{\text{Feb}}, \dots, \alpha_{\text{Dec}}$ with $\sum_m \alpha_m = 0$:
\[ y_t = \alpha_{\text{month}(t)} + E_t. \]

\textbf{2. Moving averages.} For monthly data, $\mathrm{MA}(12)$:
\[ y_t^{\text{deseason.}} = \frac{0.5\, y_{t-6} + y_{t-5} + \dots + y_{t+5} + 0.5\, y_{t+6}}{12}. \]

nodes.title: SES: no uncertainty, multi-dim P_t
Statistical model = joint law
nodes.content:
$\to$ Defining a \textbf{statistical model} for a stoch.\ process means specifying the joint probability law of $(Y_t)$, i.e.\ specifying
\[ P(Y_1, \dots, Y_n) \]
for any $n$ and any $t_1, \dots, t_n$.

Given the model, the \textbf{predictive distribution} is
\[ p(y_{t+1} \mid y_{1:t}). \]
From this we can compute summaries: $E(Y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t})$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t})$, intervals, etc.

nodes.title: Prob law via finite-dim. distributions
nodes.content:
The prob.\ law of a stoch.\ process $(Y_t)$ is assigned by giving the \textbf{finite-dimensional distributions}
\[ p_{t_1,\dots,t_n}(y_1,\dots,y_n) \]
for all $n$ and $(t_1,\dots,t_n)$.

Under \textbf{consistency} conditions, this fully defines the law of the process.

nodes.title: Forecasting algorithms — Case 0: SES
Case 1: Trend, no seasonality (Holt)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CASE 1:}} Trend / Growth, No Seasonality $\to$ \fbox{Holt-Winters}

Forecast function:
\[ f_t(h) = L_t + B_t\, h, \qquad h = 1, 2, \dots \]
where the forecasts for the level $L_t$ and the growth $B_t$ are recursively updated:
\[ L_t = \alpha\, y_t + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1}) \]
\[ B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1} \]

$L_{t-1} + B_{t-1} = \hat{y}_{t\mid t-1}$ (same as SES update).

$L_t - L_{t-1}$: growth estimate at time $t$; $B_{t-1}$: growth estimate at $t-1$.

nodes.title: Case 2: Trend + Seasonality (Holt-Winters)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{CASE 2:}} Trend + Seasonality $\to$ \fbox{Holt-Winters} full

E.g.\ monthly data, seasonal factor $S_t \approx S_{t+12} \approx S_{t+24}$.

Forecast function:
\[ \hat{y}_{t+h \mid t} = L_t + B_t\, h + S_{t+m+h}. \]

\[ L_t = \alpha\,(y_t - S_{t-m}) + (1-\alpha)\,(L_{t-1} + B_{t-1}) \]
\[ B_t = \beta\,(L_t - L_{t-1}) + (1-\beta)\, B_{t-1} \]
\[ S_t = \gamma\,(y_t - (L_{t-1} + B_{t-1})) + (1-\gamma)\, S_{t-12} \]

Three smoothing parameters $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ (level, growth, seasonality).

nodes.title: Special cases of α (SES)
nodes.content:
If $\alpha = 1$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} = y_t$ \quad (naive forecast = last obs).

If $\alpha = 0$: $\hat{y}_{t+1\mid t} = \hat{y}_{t\mid t-1}$ \quad (constant forecast, ignore new data).

In practice tune $\alpha$ on a training sample, e.g.\ minimize MSE.

nodes.title: Tuning α via predictive performance
Stationarity (2nd-order / weak)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STATIONARITY}}

A time series $(Y_t)$ is \textbf{stationary} (2nd-order / weak) if $E(Y_t)$ and $E(Y_t Y_{t+h})$ exist, are finite, and do not depend on $t$, for every $h = 1, 2, \dots$

\[ \mu(t) = \mu \quad \text{(constant mean)} \]
\[ \sigma^2(t) = \sigma^2 \quad \text{(constant variance)} \]
\[ \gamma(t, t+h) = \tilde\gamma(h) \quad \text{(autocov.\ depends on lag $h$ only)} \]

nodes.title: Stationarity does not imply strict stat.
Strict stationarity
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{STRICT STATIONARITY}}

A time series $(Y_t)$ is \textbf{strictly stationary} if the joint distribution of $(Y_t, Y_{t+1}, \dots, Y_{t+h})$ does \emph{not} depend on $t$, for any $h$:
\[ (Y_{t_1}, \dots, Y_{t_k}) \stackrel{d}{=} (Y_{t_1+h}, \dots, Y_{t_k+h}). \]

$\Rightarrow$ marginal of $Y_t$ same for all $t$:\quad $Y_1 \stackrel{d}{=} Y_2 \stackrel{d}{=} \dots$

$\Rightarrow$ if 2nd moments finite: $\mu(t) = \mu$, $\sigma^2(t) = \sigma^2$, and $\gamma(t, t+h)$ depends only on $h$.

\textbf{Strictly stationary} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{stationary}, but not the converse.

nodes.title: Most trivial example of stoch. process
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{MOST TRIVIAL EXAMPLE OF STOCH.\ PROCESS}}

Say $Y_t,\ t \ge 0$ are independent. If, additionally, $Y_t$ have a common distribution (i.i.d.) with $p$:
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p(y_1)\, p(y_2) \cdots p(y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i). \]
If only indep.\ (not necessarily identically distrib.):
\[ p_n(y_1,\dots,y_n) = p_1(y_1)\, p_2(y_2) \cdots p_n(y_n). \]

Not realistic for a time series (no temporal dependence), but it is an important building block.

\textit{Ex.:} $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ \quad Gaussian white noise.

nodes.title: Markov chain — DAG view
nodes.content:
\textbf{Markov chain on a directed acyclic graph (DAG)}

\[ Y_0 \to Y_1 \to Y_2 \to \dots \to Y_{t-1} \to Y_t \to \dots \]

Markov property: if you remove $Y_{t-1}$, then $Y_t$ and $(Y_0,\dots,Y_{t-2})$ are disconnected, i.e.\ conditionally independent given $Y_{t-1}$.

The set $\mathcal{Y}$ of the possible values of $Y_t$ is called the \textbf{state space} of the Markov chain.

nodes.title: Markov chain — definition
Transition matrix P
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{red}{TRANSITION MATRIX}}\ $\mathbf{P}$

For finite state space $\mathcal{Y} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}$:

\[ \mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} p_{1,1} & p_{1,2} & \cdots & p_{1,N} \\ p_{2,1} & p_{2,2} & \cdots & p_{2,N} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ p_{N,1} & p_{N,2} & \cdots & p_{N,N} \end{pmatrix} \]

Each row sums to 1: $\sum_{j} p_{i,j} = 1\ \forall i$.

If $\mathbf{P}_t \equiv \mathbf{P}$ (independent of $t$) $\to$ \textbf{homogeneous} Markov chain.

nodes.title: Example 1: independent Bernoulli trials
nodes.content:
\textbf{Example 1.} Independent trials $Y_t \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}$ Bernoulli$(p)$.

Transition matrix:
\[ \begin{array}{c|cc} t-1 \backslash t & 0 & 1 \\ \hline 0 & 1-p & p \\ 1 & 1-p & p \end{array} \]

\textit{(rows identical: independence!)}

nodes.title: Example 2: categorical time series
nodes.content:
\textbf{Example 2.} Markov chain as statistical model for categorical time series.

Is a Markov chain a suitable stat.\ model? Two assumptions:
\begin{enumerate} \item Markov property: $Y_t$ depends only on $Y_{t-1}$ \item probability to change opinion is constant \textit{(homogeneous)} \end{enumerate}

Example transition matrix (3 states):
\[ \begin{array}{c|ccc} t-1 \backslash t & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline 1 & 0.6 & 0.3 & 0.1 \\ 2 & 0.1 & 0.7 & 0.2 \\ 3 & 0 & 0.4 & 0.6 \end{array} \]

Rows sum to 1 $\Rightarrow$ valid.

\textit{State 1 is ``persistent''} (high $p_{1,1} = 0.6$).

nodes.title: types of data
nodes.content:
\textit{The time points of measurement can be:}
\begin{itemize} \item regularly spaced (monthly, yearly, \dots) vs irregularly spaced \item missing values \item high frequency \item cathegorical \item Univariate vs Multivariate \item discrete vs continuous time \end{itemize}
